title: Agent Authorization vs. Authentication
summary: Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines access. Why agents need both, and what changes when the actor making the request isn't a person.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Authentication and authorization are not two settings on one dial. They're two systems, checked in a fixed order, and most agent incidents blamed on "access control" are one of them failing while the other did exactly what it was told.**


The web already drew this line for humans, three decades ago. A 401 means the server has no idea who's asking. A 403 means it knows exactly who's asking and refuses anyway. Two different failures, two different fixes, and nobody confuses them on a website.


Agent access control gets this blurred constantly. "Access," "permissions," "identity" become one vocabulary for two mechanisms, and an incident writeup says "access denied" without saying which of them did the denying.


That ambiguity is expensive to carry. An agent whose actions can't be reliably attributed to a verified identity is a different risk than an agent whose identity is solid but whose permissions are too wide. Fixing the wrong one leaves the real gap open.


This post draws the technical line between the two, and shows what changes when the actor making the request isn't a person.


## Overview


HTTP settled this distinction decades ago, with two status codes most engineers can recite without looking them up. Mix them up in a design review and someone corrects you on the spot. Agent governance hasn't settled the underlying idea nearly as cleanly, even where the codes themselves are borrowed correctly.


Ask why a particular agent request got stopped, and the answer routinely comes back as one flat phrase in the incident channel. That phrase covers two entirely different situations. Maybe the platform never confirmed which agent was actually asking. Maybe it confirmed the agent precisely and refused anyway, because the action sat outside what that agent is allowed to do. Those aren't two flavors of the same problem. They are different problems with different fixes, and folding them into a single incident category is how the wrong one gets patched.


We think that collapse costs more than people expect. An agent whose identity can't be pinned down with confidence is a fundamentally different liability than an agent whose credentials check out fine but whose scope was set too generously by someone in a hurry. Treat the two interchangeably and you end up hardening the layer that was never the weak one.


What follows draws a hard line between the two mechanisms, then works through the one thing an agent needs that a person usually doesn't: two identities instead of one.


**The line that matters:** authentication answers "is this actor who it claims to be." Authorization answers "should this actor be allowed to do this, right now." An agent can pass one and fail the other, and from a support ticket the two failures look identical.


## Two Questions, in Order


The order is not arbitrary. A system authenticates first and authorizes second, because authorization is a lookup keyed on identity, and you cannot look up permissions for an actor you haven't confirmed yet. Reverse the order and you're checking permissions against a guess.


For agents, that ordering catches something people rarely have to think about with humans: identity isn't fixed the way a login session is. An agent might act as itself, or on behalf of a specific employee, or be invoked by another agent acting on behalf of both. Authentication has to resolve which of those is true before authorization can mean anything at all.


Gateway Gateway --verify--> Identity Store --confirmed, or 401--> Gateway Gateway --check--> Permission Check --allow, or 403--> Gateway Gateway --result--> Agent Authentication runs first and can fail with a 401. Authorization runs second, on a confirmed identity, and can fail with a 403. -->


**Figure 1 — Authentication and authorization as two sequential checks on the same request. Each can fail on its own, and each failure has a different name.**


Get identity wrong at the first step and the permission check that follows is answering the wrong question correctly.


## Authentication: Proving the Actor


Take a marketing automation that pulls campaign performance data and pushes spend adjustments into an ad platform. Authentication is what lets the ad platform say, with confidence, that this specific request came from the campaign-optimization agent, version 4, owned by the growth team, presenting a credential unique to it. Swap in any other agent's credential and the request looks identical. That's the failure mode worth naming: a known credential says nothing about who is currently holding it.


Strong agent authentication rests on three things. Each agent gets its own identity, not a shared service account and not a borrowed human login. Its credentials belong to it alone, not copied across a fleet of similar agents. And that identity can be verified at request time and traced back to a specific owner, not just a class of agent that behaves this way.


Authentication only answers who. Whether that "who" is allowed to do anything in particular is a separate question, and mistaking a strong authentication story for a finished access story is most of what goes wrong here.


## Authorization: Bounding the Action


Take a registered legal-intake agent, fully authenticated, so the enterprise knows exactly which agent is asking. That fact alone says nothing about whether it should be able to delete a matter, export a privileged document, or just summarize an intake form. Authorization is the layer that maps a confirmed identity onto a bounded, specific set of permissions. Unlike authentication, the answer usually depends on more than identity: the action itself, the resource it targets, sometimes the size of the request.


A registered HR onboarding agent might read provisioning templates but never payroll records. A registered data-platform agent might run read queries against the warehouse but never alter a schema. A registered procurement agent might draft purchase orders under a set threshold and route anything larger to a person. In every case the identity is settled, and the answer is still conditional. That conditionality is the whole job.


## Where They Actually Differ


Authentication Authorization


Question it answers Is this actor who it claims to be? Should this actor do this, right now?


What it checks A credential against an identity record An identity against a permission set


Typical mechanism Certificates, signed tokens, mutual TLS Scopes, roles, resource-level rules


Failure reads as A 401, the system doesn't know who's asking A 403, it knows, and says no anyway


Fixing it means Issuing or rotating a credential Narrowing or widening a scope


The rows never trade places. Rotating a credential does nothing for an over-broad scope. Narrowing a scope does nothing for a shared credential three agents can present. We'd start every incident review by asking which row it belongs to, because the fix lives on that row and nowhere else.


## Two Identities, One Request


The complication specific to agents is that they rarely act purely as themselves. A scheduling agent updates a calendar for a specific employee. An expense agent files a report for a specific traveler. The tempting shortcut is to let the agent log in as the person: inherit the session, inherit the access, and disappear from the record entirely.


That shortcut is quietly corrosive. It erases the agent from the audit trail, hands it the full breadth of a human's permissions instead of a bounded set of its own, and makes it impossible to tell afterward whether a person or an agent performed a given action.


The alternative keeps two identities live on every request. The agent authenticates as itself, so its actions trace to it and not to whoever it acted for. It holds its own narrow permission set rather than inheriting the user's entire footprint. And the user relationship is preserved alongside it, so the effective access is the intersection of what the agent may do and what the user may do. One line captures all of it:


```text
Agent A attempted to update Record B
on behalf of User C
within Permission D
```


That line carries authentication (Agent A), the human relationship (User C), and authorization (Permission D). When an action can be described that completely, an incident review is a lookup. When it can't, it's a guess dressed up as a finding.


## A Password Reset, Traced Twice


Take an IT operations agent that resets passwords and unlocks accounts across a corporate directory. When it connects, it presents a credential unique to itself. Authentication confirms this is the account-recovery agent and no other.


When a help-desk technician routes a ticket to it, the agent acts on that technician's behalf, and the technician's identity travels with the request. Ask it to unlock a standard user account and authorization allows it, because that action sits inside the agent's scope regardless of which technician asked. Ask it to reset a domain administrator's credentials and authorization refuses and escalates to a person, because that action sits outside the agent's scope no matter who's asking. Same agent. Same authentication. Opposite outcomes, because authorization answers a different question each time.


Every one of those events lands in a trail naming the agent, the technician, and the permission exercised. Months later, when someone asks why an account was unlocked at two in the morning, there's an answer instead of a shrug.


## Conclusion


Knowing who the agent is and knowing what it's allowed to do are different questions, checked by different mechanisms, in a fixed order. A program that treats them as one setting eventually discovers the gap the hard way, usually during an incident review rather than a design meeting.


Keep an agent's identity distinct from the identity of the person it acts for. Give it its own narrow permissions. Preserve the relationship between the two, and record all of it. We think that's the entire discipline, and the fact that it fits in one paragraph is exactly why teams keep skipping it.


**An agent needs its actor proven and its action allowed, and neither check substitutes for the other. Both have to run against one identity it can't borrow and can't share.**
